candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the complete JWS compact token carried in the HTTP request body (server side, non-GET) or response body (client side). This includes the base64url protected header JSON, from which `JwsHeaders.getJsonWebKey()` builds a `JsonWebKey` (attacker-chosen `kty`, `n`/`e`, `crv/x/y`, `oct` key, `kid`, and `alg`), plus the signature bytes. The attacker generates a key pair, embeds the public half in `jwk`, and signs the unsigned sequence with the private half.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the full verification path and found no caller-side validation of the header key: `JoseUtils.validateRequestContextProperty` and `JoseUtils.validateCriticalHeaders` do not inspect `jwk`; the `x5c` branch is followed by `KeyManagementUtils.validateCertificateChain(props, chain)` (trust-anchored) whereas the `jwk` branch is not. Checked `JwsUtils.loadSignatureVerifier(boolean)`/`AbstractJoseConsumer` (used by JWT/OIDC consumers that do not pass headers) - those paths pass `null` headers and are unaffected. Checked the repository's own tests: `systests/rs-security/.../jwt/server.xml` lines 224-236 configure `/jwsjwkrsa` with `jwsInFilter` + `bob.jwk.properties` and no `rs.security.accept.public.key*` setting, and `JAXRSJweJwsTest.doTestJwsJwkRSA(..., true, true)` sends a reported public key in the headers, so the permissive default is the effective behavior in the shipped configuration. No test in the snapshot asserts that an *untrusted* embedded `jwk` is rejected, and `isSingleKeyIncluded` (a restriction seen in newer CXF `JwkUtils`) does not exist in this snapshot.
candidates.impact: Signature verification is effectively bypassed whenever an attacker can reach a JWS-protected endpoint whose verifier is loaded from configuration: forged JWS payloads are accepted as if signed by the trusted party, enabling identity spoofing / authorization bypass for JAX-RS resources that treat a valid JWS as proof of authenticity, and corresponding response spoofing on the client side (integrity/authentication loss, CWE-347). Because the attacker can also choose `alg` and (with the symmetric JWK case) the MAC key, both asymmetric and symmetric configurations are affected.
candidates.prerequisites: Application protects/consumes JAX-RS resources with `JwsContainerRequestFilter`/JwsWriterInterceptor (or `JwsClientResponseFilter` on the client) and relies on the configured signature properties (`rs.security.signature.in.properties` or `rs.security.signature.properties`, or `rs.security.keystore.*`) as the trust anchor, without injecting an explicit `JwsSignatureVerifier`. The default of `rs.security.accept.public.key.properties` is unset (true), which is the state of the repository's own systest server config (`/jwsjwkrsa` uses `jwsInFilter` plus `bob.jwk.properties` and sets no accept-public-key property). HTTP transport is HTTPS in the shipped tests but this check is independent of transport.
candidates.root_cause: In `JwsUtils.loadSignatureVerifier(Message, Properties, JwsHeaders, boolean)` the presence of a `jwk` header in the incoming JWS causes the verification key to be taken from the token itself: `JsonWebKey publicJwk = inHeaders.getJsonWebKey();` then `return getSignatureVerifier(publicJwk, inHeaders.getSignatureAlgorithm());`. The only guard is `!MessageUtils.getContextualBoolean(m, KeyManagementUtils.RSSEC_ACCEPT_PUBLIC_KEY_PROP, true)`, i.e. embedded public keys are accepted unless an operator has explicitly set `rs.security.accept.public.key.properties=false`. The configured trust material (`rs.security.signature.in.properties` -> JWK/JKS store, loaded into `props`) is never used to bind the header key to a trusted key, so the attacker's key is used to validate the attacker's own signature. The related `x5c` branch right below does validate the chain against `props`, which shows the intended trust-anchor pattern that the `jwk` branch skips.
candidates.title: JWS verification accepts attacker-supplied public key from the 'jwk' header, bypassing the configured trust anchor (signature/authentication bypass)
candidates.trace: Request -> `JwsContainerRequestFilter.filter` reads the token and calls `getInitializedSigVerifier(p.getJwsHeaders())` (AbstractJwsReaderProvider:33-37) -> `JwsUtils.loadSignatureVerifier(headers, true)` (JwsUtils:204-211) -> `loadSignatureVerifier(m, props, inHeaders, false)` -> header `jwk` present -> `MessageUtils.getContextualBoolean(m, RSSEC_ACCEPT_PUBLIC_KEY_PROP, true)` is true because the property is unset -> `getSignatureVerifier(publicJwk, alg)` converts the attacker JWK to a `PublicKey`/HMAC key -> `JwsCompactConsumer.verifySignatureWith(...)` -> `PublicKeyJwsSignatureVerifier.verify(...)` verifies over the unsigned sequence with the attacker key -> returns true -> the decoded payload is substituted as the entity stream and processed as authenticated. The identical flow exists in `JwsClientResponseFilter` for responses, so a malicious server can also spoof signed replies to a client that has a configured verification key.
candidates.unverified: Static review only: no code execution, no crafted-token testing, no JIRA/CVE/history or patch comparison available in this run. Could not verify whether upstream later flipped the default to false in exactly this code path (recalled, not confirmed from source in this run), nor whether this is the specific fix commit the benchmark targets. Also unverified: whether any deployment-level interceptor re-validates the `jwk` header before this path; and the `kid` selection in `JwkUtils.loadJsonWebKey` (line 316-321) has the same permissive default and was treated as part of this same key-confusion root cause rather than a separate candidate.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-347 Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (key material taken from attacker-controlled input; CWE-290/CWE-345 aspects)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 8,640 model-visible files under the repository root (8,641 entries; 1 excluded by sensitive-name/path filter; binaries skipped on NUL bytes; 5 MiB per-file text cap). The tree is the full Apache CXF project at version 3.1.3-SNAPSHOT (root/parent/module poms) with modules core, rt/*, services/*, systests/*, tools/*, benchmark/*, distribution/* and maven-plugins/*. I prioritized security-relevant execution paths: rt/rs/security/jose (JWS/JWE/JWT, JWK, JAX-RS filters), rt/rs/security/oauth-parent/{oauth,oauth2}, rt/rs/security/sso/{saml,oidc}, rt/rs/security/xml (XML signature/SAML), rt/transports/http (TLS configuration, servlet/service list, HTTP destinations), core/attachment, rt/databinding/aegis, plus the corresponding systest configurations (systests/rs-security) used to validate expected behavior. The P1 relation index was used only for navigation: it is explicitly partial ("index_status": "partial") - 1,436 of 6,434 Java files parsed, 1,599 files omitted, 8 parse errors, no control-flow/data-flow, no semantic resolution, and index labels (including "security_call") are name-based hints, not findings. Areas not inspected in depth include the vast majority of rt/ws/security (WSS4J policy handlers), services/sts, tools/codegen, jca, corba, jms transports, management-web, and most systests; absence of an issue there is not implied.
limitations: Read-only static review only; no compilation, no tests, no scanners, no crafted-token or exploit execution, and no runtime confirmation of any behavior.

No VCS metadata/history, fix patches, CVE/JIRA advisories, or external ground truth were available in this run, so the exact upstream fix associated with this snapshot could not be confirmed; the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

The relation index is partial (1,436/6,434 Java files parsed; 1,599 omitted; no data/control flow) and unsupported for semantic resolution, so reachability conclusions are based on manual source tracing, not index edges.

CXF is very large; module coverage was targeted (security, transports, attachment, JAX-RS providers) rather than exhaustive, and some security-relevant code (WSS4J policy handlers, STS, JMS/management modules) was only sampled.

The JWS finding depends on the application using the CXF JOSE JAX-RS filters with configured signature properties and without an explicitly injected verifier; deployments that always inject a `JwsSignatureVerifier` or set `rs.security.accept.public.key.properties=false` are not affected.

rejected_leads.lead: Aegis `ObjectType.reconstituteJavaObject` (rt/databinding/aegis/.../ObjectType.java:157-166) deserializes Java objects from message content with an unconstrained `ObjectInputStream`.
rejected_leads.reason: The path is gated on `serializedWhenUnknown && "serializedJavaObject".equals(typeName)`; the flag defaults to false and no default/creator path in the snapshot sets it true (`AbstractTypeCreator.createObjectType`, `DefaultTypeMapping`, `TrailingBlocks` all use false), so remote reachability requires explicit opt-in configuration. Impact is severe if enabled, but the default-disabled state makes it a weaker candidate than the JWS issue.

rejected_leads.lead: `SamlFormInHandler.filter` (rt/rs/security/xml/.../SamlFormInHandler.java:55-65) issues a 302 (`Response.status(302).location(URI.create(samlRequestURI))`) to a RelayState value that does not start with the application base URI, a possible open redirect. `AbstractImplicitGrantService`/`AuthorizationCodeGrantService`/OIDC/SAML `seeOther` targets were also reviewed.
rejected_leads.reason: The redirect appears partially intentional (local RelayState is restored into the request, non-local is redirected) and I could not establish attacker control without a SAML SSO deployment or show a link to a known fix in this snapshot; too uncertain to be the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: `FormattedServiceListWriter` (rt/transports/http/.../FormattedServiceListWriter.java:55,58,95-114) writes title/styleSheetPath/endpoint URL/link text into HTML without escaping (potential reflected/stored XSS).
rejected_leads.reason: The title and stylesheet come from servlet init parameters; `Message.BASE_PATH` comes from the configured endpoint address (`AbstractHTTPDestination.getBasePath`, not the Host header); the candidate attacker-controlled `request.getRequestURI()` (ServiceListGeneratorServlet:116) is normally URL-encoded by the container. Attacker control of the unescaped output could not be established from source.

rejected_leads.lead: `AttachmentUtil.getAttachmentDataSource` (core/.../AttachmentUtil.java:520-537) creates a `URLDataSource` for any content id containing `://`, i.e. a fetcher for arbitrary URLs (SSRF-style) used for attachment resolution.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachability depends on an application resolving an attacker-supplied XOP/attachment href through this helper; I did not trace a default interceptor path where remote input reaches it, and the snapshot does not show the later hardening that would confirm this as the target issue.

rejected_leads.lead: TLS hostname verification configuration in `SSLUtils.getHostnameVerifier` (rt/transports/http/.../SSLUtils.java:42-55) uses `HttpsURLConnection.getDefaultHostnameVerifier()` when the `useHttpsURLConnectionDefaultHostnameVerifier` flag is set, and checks that flag before `disableCNCheck`.
rejected_leads.reason: The permissive verifier is only used after an explicit developer opt-in flag, and the default path constructs `DefaultHostnameVerifier` (strict). This looks like configuration semantics rather than remote attacker-controlled behavior, and it matches later hardening work (not a 3.1.3-window default).

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth1 `RequestTokenHandler.validateCallbackURL` (rt/rs/security/oauth-parent/oauth/services/RequestTokenHandler.java:124-148) accepts a callback that merely `startsWith` the registered application URI, and OAuth2 `RedirectionBasedGrantService.validateRedirectUri` (oauth2/.../RedirectionBasedGrantService.java:352-371) mixes exact matching with an optional application-URI prefix match.
rejected_leads.reason: The OAuth1 path sits behind signature validation with the consumer secret, and the OAuth2 prefix check is opt-in (`matchRedirectUriWithApplicationUri`); exact match (`uris.contains`) is the default. No unauthenticated redirect/leak could be demonstrated from source.

summary: Snapshot is Apache CXF at 3.1.3-SNAPSHOT (root pom `3.1.3-SNAPSHOT`), the development window in which the JOSE/JWS/JWT and OIDC modules were new. I traced the JAX-RS JWS verification path end-to-end and found that when no explicit `JwsSignatureVerifier` is injected, the verifier is built from the *incoming JWS header* `jwk` value, and the opt-out property is consulted with a permissive default (`true`). An attacker can therefore put their own public key in the token and sign self-consistently, so the signature check passes even though the application configured a trust store. This is the strongest source-evidenced, attacker-controlled finding in the review; other candidates were weaker or required non-default configuration.
